title: What If You Were 10x Stronger?
hook: You open a pickle jar and the lid goes through the ceiling.
rule: Only your muscles got stronger. Your bones and tendons didn't. Pull too hard, and you break yourself.
beats: Moving day: you carry the sofa, the fridge, and your cousin
Handshakes become dangerous, so you practice holding eggs
You lift a weight and feel your own tendon start to give
climax: A car rolls back onto your friend Leo's leg in a parking lot. Lifting it could snap your arm. Your arm... or Leo.
ending: You lift it, Leo slides out, and you both end up with matching casts. He signs yours: 'Strongest idiot I know.'
loop: Ends in the kitchen with a new pickle jar.
facts: Your nervous system holds your muscles back from their maximum force, partly to protect your tendons and bones
There are real reports of people lifting cars in emergencies, a burst of adrenaline-fueled strength
visuals: kitchen ceiling hole, moving truck, eggs, gym, parking lot

title: What If You Never Blinked Again?
opening: What If You Never Blinked Again? Then: You win every staring contest before it starts.
early_wins: You start seeing things nobody else notices: a card trick's secret move, a bird landing.
mystery_and_reveal: You blink about fifteen times a minute, so your eyes are shut for roughly a tenth of your waking day, and your brain hides those gaps so the world never goes dark. Except now your eyes dry out and sting all day.
climax: Your little brother's school play: you can sit there with burning eyes and see every second of it, or look away and rest.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: Most people blink around 15 to 20 times a minute
The brain hides blinks so the world doesn't seem to flicker

title: What If You Could Smell 10,000x Better?
hook: Your friend swears he didn't eat your fries. You lean in, sniff once... and you can smell ketchup on his breath, his lie, and the dog he petted three hours ago.
rule: You can't turn it off. Every smell, all the time, at full volume.
beats: You smell rain coming twenty minutes before it hits
You find your lost phone by smelling your own hand cream on it
Garbage day becomes a horror movie; the school bus is a war crime
climax: On the night of your big interview you smell rotten eggs drifting from your neighbor's house: a gas leak, and they're asleep. Make the interview... or bang on their door.
ending: You wake them up, the gas company finds the leak, and the next day the neighbor brings fries to say thank you. Your friend eats them.
loop: Ends on the friend eating your fries again, which opens the video.
facts: A dog's nose is estimated to be 10,000 to 100,000 times more sensitive than ours
Natural gas has no smell; companies add a rotten-egg smell so people notice leaks
visuals: diner, smell trails drawn as colored wisps, rain cloud, garbage truck, night street, gas wisps

title: What If Your Heart Beat Only Six Times a Minute?
opening: What If Your Heart Beat Only Six Times a Minute? Then: Your doctor checks your pulse, frowns, and checks again.
early_wins: You can hold your breath forever, but standing up too fast makes you black out.
mystery_and_reveal: A blue whale's heart can drop to about two beats a minute on a dive, but its blood is built for it. Yours isn't, so your brain keeps running short of blood.
climax: Your friend collapses at a party and needs CPR. Rushing in could make you faint too.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: A blue whale's heart can slow to around 2 beats per minute during a dive
Standing up quickly can make you dizzy because blood briefly drains from the brain

title: What If You Grew 10x Taller?
hook: You step over a bus to get to school. Not onto it. Over it.
rule: Ten times taller means about a thousand times heavier, but your bones only get a hundred times stronger. Every step is a fight against your own weight.
beats: You change a streetlight bulb for the whole street
Your legs ache constantly, every step like carrying ten people
Clothes need a tailor and a crane; lunch needs a truck
climax: A kid's kite tangles a little girl on a balcony ledge, high up. Reaching her means kneeling on your knee in a way your bones may not survive. Protect your legs... or reach.
ending: You reach, she's safe, and your knee holds. Barely. She ties the kite to your finger like a balloon.
loop: Ends with you stepping carefully over the bus on the way home.
facts: Scale an animal up 10x and its weight grows about 1,000x while bone strength only grows about 100x (the square-cube law)
The tallest man ever measured, at about 2.72 meters, needed leg braces to walk
visuals: tiny city, bus at ankle height, streetlight, crane, balcony

title: What If You Felt Everyone Else's Pain?
opening: What If You Felt Everyone Else's Pain? Then: Your friend stubs his toe, and you're the one hopping around the kitchen.
early_wins: You always know who's hurting, even when they're hiding it, and nobody can lie to you about being fine.
mystery_and_reveal: A small number of people really feel touches they only see happening to others. It's called mirror-touch synesthesia. Now crowds, sports and hospitals are unbearable.
climax: Your mom needs someone with her during a painful procedure. Going means feeling all of it.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: Mirror-touch synesthesia is real: some people feel a touch when they see someone else being touched

title: What If You Could Never Forget Anything?
hook: Your teacher asks what she wore on the first day of school three years ago. You tell her. And the color of her socks.
rule: You remember everything. Including everything you'd love to forget.
beats: Every test is easy, you remember every word of every page
You remember every embarrassing moment in full HD, forever
Arguments are impossible to win against you, and nobody wants to argue with you anymore
climax: At the national quiz final, your best friend Mia is having a panic attack backstage. Win the trophy you've trained for... or walk off stage to sit with her.
ending: You sit with her, she calms down, and years later she still thanks you. You remember exactly what she said. That one, you'd never want to forget.
loop: Ends back in class with the teacher asking another impossible question.
facts: A rare condition called hyperthymesia lets a few people recall almost every day of their lives
Forgetting is useful: the brain actively prunes memories so the important ones stand out
visuals: classroom, floating memory 'photos', quiz show stage, backstage

title: What If You Could See Sounds as Colors?
opening: What If You Could See Sounds as Colors? Then: Your alarm goes off and your whole room turns orange.
early_wins: Music becomes a light show. You can 'see' who's calling by the color of their ringtone.
mystery_and_reveal: Some people really do see colors when they hear sounds. It's a form of synesthesia, and several famous musicians have described it. But loud places become blinding.
climax: At a fireworks festival your little brother gets lost in the crowd. The noise is a wall of color, but his voice is a color you'd know anywhere.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: Chromesthesia, seeing colors when hearing sounds, is a real form of synesthesia

title: What If You Never Needed Sleep Again?
hook: It's three in the morning and you've already finished your homework, learned guitar, and reorganised the fridge.
rule: You never get tired, but everyone you love still does. Your extra eight hours are spent alone.
beats: You get a whole extra day every week
The record for staying awake is about eleven days, and you passed it a month ago
Three a.m. gets lonely: no one to text, empty streets
climax: At 3 a.m. you smell smoke from the apartment below. Finish the competition entry due at 6... or wake up the whole building.
ending: You bang on every door, everyone gets out, and the firefighter says the building was lucky someone was awake. For once, being the only one awake was the point.
loop: Ends at 3 a.m. again, you wide awake, everyone asleep.
facts: The record for staying awake, set in 1964, is about 11 days
Scientists found the brain clears out waste while we sleep
visuals: night bedroom, clock, guitar, empty street, apartment hallway, smoke

title: What If You Could See Heat?
opening: What If You Could See Heat? Then: You can tell which seat on the bus someone just got up from.
early_wins: You see who's nervous (warm face), which coffee is still hot, and footprints glowing on the floor.
mystery_and_reveal: Pit vipers really sense heat through little pits on their faces, which is how they hunt in total darkness. But for you, every lamp and car engine glares like the sun.
climax: In a smoke-filled building, everyone is blind except you, and you can see a small warm shape behind a door.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: Pit vipers detect infrared heat with pit organs on their faces

title: What If You Shrank to the Size of an Ant?
hook: You fall off the kitchen table... and float down to the floor like a leaf, completely fine.
rule: Small bodies lose heat fast. You're always freezing, and always hungry.
beats: Falls can't hurt you; you jump off the bookshelf for fun
A raindrop hits you like a bucket of water
You need to eat constantly just to stay warm
climax: Your dog is choking on a tiny piece of plastic stuck where no hand can reach. You can climb in and pull it out, but it's dark, wet and terrifying. Stay safe... or save the dog.
ending: You pull it free and the dog sneezes you across the room onto a pillow. Best ride of your life.
loop: Ends falling off the table again, floating down.
facts: Insects can survive falls from almost any height because air resistance slows small bodies so much
Small animals lose body heat much faster, which is why shrews have to eat almost constantly
visuals: giant kitchen, floating fall, raindrop splash, dog's huge face

title: What If You Remembered Being a Baby?
opening: What If You Remembered Being a Baby? Then: You remember your own first birthday party. The cake. Who cried. Who didn't come.
early_wins: At family dinners you correct everyone's stories, and you remember things your parents hoped you'd forget.
mystery_and_reveal: Almost nobody remembers anything before about age three. Scientists call it infantile amnesia, and part of it is that the baby brain is still building the system that stores memories.
climax: Your dad has always felt guilty about something from when you were one. You remember what really happened, and it wasn't his fault.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: Most adults remember almost nothing from before about age 3 or 4

title: What If You Aged 10x Slower?
hook: You're forty years old and the cinema still won't sell you a ticket to a scary movie.
rule: You age slowly. Everyone you love doesn't.
beats: Your childhood dog grows old while you're still a kid
Your little sister becomes your older sister
You'd have centuries to learn everything, but no one to share them with
climax: Your grandma's last wish is to see you graduate, but at your speed that's decades away. Keep the rule of your life... or do a crash course, cramming years of learning into months, for her.
ending: You graduate in record time. She's in the front row, cheering louder than anyone, and the photo stays on your wall for the next three hundred years.
loop: Ends at the cinema ticket desk again.
facts: Greenland sharks can live for centuries, possibly over 400 years
Different animals age at very different speeds: a mouse lives about 2 years, a bowhead whale over 200
visuals: cinema desk, dog aging, sister growing, graduation stage, grandma

title: What If You Could Control Every Dream?
opening: What If You Could Control Every Dream? Then: Every night, you fly. Every single night.
early_wins: You practise piano in your dreams and wake up better at it. But real life starts feeling dull.
mystery_and_reveal: Lucid dreaming is real: about half of people have had at least one dream where they knew they were dreaming. But your dreams get so good you stop wanting to wake up.
climax: Your best friend needs you awake at 3 a.m. for an emergency, in the middle of the best dream you've ever had.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: About half of people report having had at least one lucid dream

title: What If You Could Hear 100x Better?
hook: In a silent exam hall, you can hear every heartbeat. The kid next to you is panicking, and his heart is racing.
rule: Quiet sounds get loud, and loud sounds get unbearable.
beats: You hear whispers three classrooms away
You hear your microwave ding from across town
A fire truck siren feels like being punched in the ears
climax: After a building collapses on TV, rescuers ask for total silence. You can hear faint tapping under the rubble, but standing that close to the sirens and machines could permanently damage your hearing. Your hearing... or a stranger.
ending: You find the tapping, they're rescued, and the first thing they say is 'thank you'. You hear it perfectly.
loop: Ends back in the silent exam hall with heartbeats.
facts: Humans hear roughly 20 to 20,000 hertz; dogs hear far higher pitches
Sounds around 120 decibels start to cause pain
visuals: exam hall, heartbeat icons, sound waves, siren, rubble

title: What If You Weighed 10x Less?
opening: What If You Weighed 10x Less? Then: You jump to catch a frisbee and come down three seconds later.
early_wins: You can stand on a branch, bounce over fences, carry friends on your back.
mystery_and_reveal: On the Moon you'd weigh about a sixth of what you weigh here. Ten times lighter than that, and a strong gust of wind becomes the most dangerous thing in your life.
climax: On a windy cliff walk, your little brother slips toward the edge. Grabbing him means letting go of the railing you're holding onto.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: On the Moon you weigh about one-sixth of your Earth weight

title: What If Your Body Healed 100x Faster?
hook: You get a paper cut, and it closes before the blood even reaches your fingertip.
rule: Healing takes energy. Healing 100x faster means you're hungry all the time.
beats: Scraped knees heal before you stand up
You eat six meals before lunch
You break a finger and it heals before anyone can straighten it, so it's crooked forever
climax: Your friend Mia needs blood after an accident and you're a match. Giving blood will leave you weak and starving before the big race. The race... or Mia.
ending: You give it, she recovers, and she brings you the biggest sandwich in the world. You finish it in four bites.
loop: Ends with another paper cut.
facts: Healing burns extra energy and protein, which is why recovering patients need more food
A broken bone that heals in the wrong position stays that way unless it's broken and reset
visuals: paper cut, plates of food, finger splint, hospital, sandwich

title: What If You Never Felt Hungry Again?
opening: What If You Never Felt Hungry Again? Then: You forget lunch. Then dinner. Then breakfast.
early_wins: You save so much time and money, and you never get grumpy.
mystery_and_reveal: Hunger is a signal: a hormone called ghrelin, made mostly in your stomach, tells your brain it's time to eat. Without that alarm, your body runs out of fuel and nothing warns you.
climax: On the day of your big final, you faint, and your friend Mia has to choose between finishing her own exam and helping you.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: Ghrelin, a hormone mostly made in the stomach, is often called the hunger hormone

title: What If You Never Felt Fear?
hook: You pet a shark. On purpose. And you smile while doing it.
rule: Fear is what keeps you alive. Without it, you have no brakes.
beats: Roller coasters are boring; public speaking is easy
You walk up to a growling dog to say hi, and get bitten
Your friends stop letting you drive
climax: Your little brother Sam is stuck on a roof during a storm. You'd climb without a second thought, but no fear also means no caution. Rush in... or slow down and do it right.
ending: For the first time, you choose to be careful. You use the ladder, tie the rope and bring Sam down safe. Turns out bravery isn't having no fear; it's choosing how to act.
loop: Ends at the aquarium, a shark swimming past.
facts: Fear is driven largely by a small brain region called the amygdala
A real patient with a damaged amygdala walked up to snakes and spiders without fear
visuals: aquarium, roller coaster, stage, dog, storm, roof, ladder

title: What If Your Body Glowed in the Dark?
opening: What If Your Body Glowed in the Dark? Then: Lights off, and you're the night light.
early_wins: You never need a torch, and your sleepovers are legendary.
mystery_and_reveal: Here's the weird part: your body already glows. Scientists in Japan photographed it, about a thousand times too faint for your eyes to see. Turn that up, and you can never hide in the dark.
climax: During hide and seek at night, a little kid gets lost in the woods. You're the only one he can follow.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: The human body emits visible light about 1,000 times too weak for our eyes to see (measured in a 2009 study in Japan)

title: What If You Could See in the Dark?
hook: The power goes out at a sleepover. Everyone screams. You calmly walk over and hand everyone a snack.
rule: Eyes built for darkness are crushed by bright light. Sunlight is blinding.
beats: You read comics under the blanket with no torch
Daylight hurts, so you wear sunglasses even indoors
In photos your eyes glow like a cat's
climax: A stadium loses power during a match, and thousands panic in the dark. Guiding people out means facing the emergency floodlights when they come back on. Your eyes... or the crowd.
ending: You guide a whole section out safely, then the lights snap on and everything goes white. When your eyes recover, the first thing you see is a crowd clapping.
loop: Ends at the sleepover when the lights go out again.
facts: Cats can see in about one-sixth of the light humans need
Your eyes take around 20 to 30 minutes to fully adjust to darkness
visuals: dark bedroom drawn in blue tones, glowing eyes, stadium, floodlights

title: What If Your Skin Couldn't Be Cut?
opening: What If Your Skin Couldn't Be Cut? Then: You trip onto broken glass and stand up without a scratch.
early_wins: Bike crashes, kitchen knives, cactus hugs: nothing gets through.
mystery_and_reveal: But doctors can't get through either. No injections, no stitches, no surgery. Skin is your body's largest organ and its main shield, and yours now shields you from help too.
climax: Your appendix is about to burst, and the only way in is... there isn't one. Or is there?
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: Skin is the body's largest organ

title: What If Your Memory Reset Every Day?
hook: You wake up and there's a note on your hand in your own handwriting: 'Read this first. Don't panic.'
rule: Every morning, yesterday is gone. But skills stay, even when the memories don't.
beats: Your room is covered in sticky notes you wrote to yourself
You play piano perfectly but can't remember learning
Every day, you meet your best friend for the first time
climax: Today is Mom's birthday. You find a half-finished gift you've been building in secret for weeks, with no memory of it. Finish it from your notes... or give up and buy something.
ending: You follow your own notes, finish it, and Mom cries. You won't remember tonight, so you write one more note: 'She loved it.'
loop: Ends with you writing on your hand, the note from the opening.
facts: People who can't form new memories can still learn new skills, like drawing or puzzles, without remembering practising
Memories are formed with help from a brain region called the hippocampus
visuals: hand note, sticky notes wall, piano, gift box, birthday cake

title: What If You Had No Fingerprints?
opening: What If You Had No Fingerprints? Then: Your phone refuses to recognize you. So does the airport.
early_wins: Mystery novels hate you. Every border crossing takes three hours.
mystery_and_reveal: A tiny number of families really are born without fingerprints. Doctors nicknamed it 'immigration delay disease'. Fingerprints also help your fingers grip.
climax: Your friend is wrongly blamed for something based on fingerprints at the scene, and you're the only one who can prove how fingerprints actually work.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: A very rare condition called adermatoglyphia means people are born without fingerprints

title: What If Your Voice Was 100x Louder?
hook: You sneeze in the library. Every window in the building shatters.
rule: You can't turn it down. Whispering is your new full volume.
beats: You call your friend from across the city without a phone
Singing in the shower sets off car alarms
Nobody invites you to the movies anymore
climax: On a ski trip you spot a group of hikers walking toward an avalanche zone, too far away to reach. Shouting could save them, but it could also shake loose the snow above you. Stay quiet... or shout.
ending: You aim the shout carefully, they turn around, and the snow holds. They wave. You wave back, quietly.
loop: Ends in the library, feeling a sneeze coming.
facts: Sound can shatter glass when it hits the glass's exact resonant frequency loudly enough
A jet engine up close is about 140 decibels, enough to damage hearing instantly
visuals: library, shattering glass, sound rings, mountain, avalanche

title: What If You Could Hear Your Eyes Move?
opening: What If You Could Hear Your Eyes Move? Then: You look left. Something in your head goes 'shhk'.
early_wins: You hear your own heartbeat, your footsteps echo inside your skull, and chewing sounds like an avalanche.
mystery_and_reveal: This is real: a tiny hole in the bone of the inner ear can let people hear their own eyeballs moving. Now silence doesn't exist for you.
climax: In a silent exam hall you can hear a classmate's quiet, panicked breathing. Say something, or stay focused on your own test.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: Superior canal dehiscence, a thin spot in the inner-ear bone, can make people hear their own eye movements and heartbeat

title: What If You Could Never Feel Cold?
hook: Everyone's shivering at the frozen lake. You're swimming in shorts, eating ice cream.
rule: You can't feel cold, but your body still freezes. Nothing warns you.
beats: Snowball fights are your sport now
You save a fortune on jackets
Your fingers turn white and you don't notice until a friend grabs your hand
climax: A dog falls through the ice. You're the only one who doesn't hesitate, but cold water can make you lose control of your arms within minutes. Stay on shore... or go in, knowing your clock is running.
ending: You go in, grab the dog and get out with seconds to spare. Then everyone wraps you in every blanket they own, and the dog won't leave your side.
loop: Ends back in the frozen lake with ice cream.
facts: In icy water there's a '1-10-1' rule: about 1 minute to control your breathing, 10 minutes of useful movement, and up to an hour before you pass out
Frostbite can start without pain once the area goes numb
visuals: frozen lake, ice cream, snowball fight, cracked ice, blankets

title: What If You Had Perfect Pitch?
opening: What If You Had Perfect Pitch? Then: The microwave beeps and you say, 'That's a B flat.'
early_wins: You can sing any note, tune any guitar, and name every car horn.
mystery_and_reveal: Only about one person in ten thousand has perfect pitch. But it means every slightly out-of-tune song is physically painful to listen to.
climax: Your best friend asks you to judge her first live performance, and she's a little off key. Honest, or kind?
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: Perfect pitch is estimated to occur in about 1 in 10,000 people

title: What If You Only Ate Once a Year?
hook: It's your one meal day. You start with forty pizzas. That's the appetizer.
rule: A whole year of energy has to fit in one day. That's around seven hundred thousand calories.
beats: You save hours every day, no breakfast, no lunch
Every dinner party is awkward because you just sit there
Your meal day costs as much as a car
climax: Your best friend's wedding lands on your one meal day. Eat your year's food... or give the toast you promised.
ending: You give the toast, people cry, and the chef sends a whole buffet to your table afterwards. Everyone watches you eat it like a sport.
loop: Ends with the next meal day starting, pizza boxes stacked to the ceiling.
facts: An average adult needs roughly two thousand calories a day, about seven hundred thousand a year
A normal stomach holds about a litre comfortably but can stretch to around four
visuals: pizza tower, calendar, dinner party, wedding, buffet

title: What If You Were Allergic to Water?
opening: What If You Were Allergic to Water? Then: Rain is your enemy. So is the shower.
early_wins: You become an expert at wet wipes and umbrellas, and swimming is gone forever.
mystery_and_reveal: An extremely rare condition makes skin break out in itchy hives when it touches water, even your own sweat or tears. So crying hurts.
climax: Your little brother falls into a pool and nobody else sees. Jumping in means hours of burning skin.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: Aquagenic urticaria, a reaction to water on the skin, is extremely rare

title: What If You Could Run at 100 km/h?
hook: You miss the bus. You're waiting at the next stop when it arrives.
rule: Your legs are fast. Your shoes, your lungs and the air aren't ready.
beats: Shoes melt in a week
At that speed, air pushes against you like a storm
Bugs hit your face like tiny rocks
climax: An ambulance is stuck in traffic and your friend Leo needs his allergy medicine across town now. Running there means destroying your knees on the road. Your knees... or Leo.
ending: You get there in time, Leo's fine, and you limp home in borrowed slippers. Leo pays for the bus.
loop: Ends at the bus stop again, the bus pulling away.
facts: Usain Bolt's top speed was about 44 kilometers per hour
When you run, each foot hits the ground with several times your body weight
visuals: bus, speed lines, melting shoes, traffic jam, ambulance

title: What If You Could Smell Diseases?
opening: What If You Could Smell Diseases? Then: You hug your grandpa and something smells wrong.
early_wins: You can smell a cold coming, a fever starting, someone who's stressed.
mystery_and_reveal: A woman in Scotland noticed her husband's smell changed years before he was diagnosed with Parkinson's, and scientists later confirmed the disease really has a smell. But how do you tell someone what you smelled?
climax: You smell it on your teacher, who seems totally fine. Say something and look crazy, or say nothing.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: A woman in Scotland could smell Parkinson's disease, and researchers have since studied the scent

title: What If You Could Taste 100x Stronger?
hook: You sip a glass of milk and say, 'This cow was stressed.'
rule: Every flavour is turned up a hundred times. Most food is too much.
beats: You become the world's best chef overnight
Coffee tastes like drinking lightning
A single chili flake makes you cry
climax: At a wedding you taste a tiny trace of peanut in the cake. Your best friend Mia has a severe peanut allergy and is about to take a bite. Stay polite... or embarrass the host in front of everyone.
ending: You knock the fork out of her hand. The host checks, and the baker did use peanut oil. Mia buys you dessert. You can taste exactly how grateful she is.
loop: Ends with another glass of milk.
facts: About a quarter of people are 'supertasters', who taste bitterness much more strongly
Most people have a few thousand taste buds
visuals: milk glass, chef kitchen, chili flake, wedding cake

title: What If You Could Never Get Sick?
opening: What If You Could Never Get Sick? Then: Your whole class is out with flu. You show up with soup for everyone.
early_wins: Perfect attendance. You lick a subway pole for a dare.
mystery_and_reveal: But a stronger immune system isn't always better. Allergies are your immune system overreacting, and an immune system that's too aggressive can start attacking your own body.
climax: A new illness spreads through your town, and scientists want your blood to study. It means months of tests instead of the trip of your life.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: Allergies are the immune system overreacting to something harmless

title: What If Your Brain Worked 10x Harder?
hook: You solve the Rubik's cube your friend handed you before he finishes saying 'try this'.
rule: Your brain already uses a fifth of your energy. Ten times more means you overheat and starve.
beats: Homework takes seconds
You eat constantly and still lose weight
You get headaches from overheating, so you study with ice on your head
climax: A blackout hits the hospital during a storm and the backup system is failing. You can figure out the fix, but thinking that hard for that long could make you pass out. The quiz scholarship exam tomorrow... or the hospital.
ending: You fix it and wake up in the same hospital, with a nurse handing you a giant plate of food. Best meal of your life.
loop: Ends with a Rubik's cube in your hands.
facts: The brain is about 2% of your body weight but uses about 20% of your energy
The idea that we only use 10% of our brain is a myth
visuals: Rubik's cube, ice pack, food, hospital, glowing brain icon

title: What If You Never Forgot a Face?
opening: What If You Never Forgot a Face? Then: You spot your kindergarten teacher in a crowd of thousands, twenty years later.
early_wins: Strangers seem familiar because you really have seen them before, once, on a bus, in 2019.
mystery_and_reveal: A small group of people called super-recognizers can do this, and some police forces actually hire them. But you can't forget anyone, including the bully.
climax: A lost child's photo is on the news, and you're sure you saw that face at the train station this morning.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: Super-recognizers, roughly the top 1-2% at remembering faces, are used by some police forces

title: What If You Could Breathe Underwater?
hook: You take a nap at the bottom of a swimming pool. The lifeguard does not take it well.
rule: Water holds far less oxygen than air. You need to keep moving water over your gills, and on land your skin dries out.
beats: You explore coral reefs for hours
Out of the water you need a spray bottle every ten minutes
A hot day is your worst nightmare
climax: A diver gets tangled in a fishing net deep underwater, running out of air. Freeing him means staying down long after your skin starts to hurt from the cold. Your comfort... or a stranger.
ending: You free him and share a smile through his mask. Back on the beach he hands you his water bottle. You pour it on your head.
loop: Ends at the bottom of the pool, eyes closing for a nap.
facts: Water holds dozens of times less oxygen than the same amount of air
Fish breathe by pushing water over their gills, which is why many can't stop swimming
visuals: pool bottom, gills, coral, spray bottle, fishing net, beach

title: What If You Couldn't Recognize Faces?
opening: What If You Couldn't Recognize Faces? Then: Your own mom walks past you in the supermarket, and you don't know her.
early_wins: You learn people by their shoes, their laugh, the way they walk.
mystery_and_reveal: About one person in fifty has some face blindness, called prosopagnosia. They see faces fine, but their brain can't tell them apart.
climax: At your graduation, everyone looks the same, and you have to find your dad in a crowd before he leaves.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: Face blindness (prosopagnosia) affects roughly 2% of people to some degree

title: What If Your Eyes Could Zoom 100x?
hook: You read your friend's text from across the stadium. He's typing 'don't tell anyone'.
rule: You see everything. Including what you really shouldn't.
beats: You spot a bird's nest on a skyscraper roof
Eye strain gives you headaches after an hour
You accidentally see your surprise party planning three blocks away
climax: At the beach, you spot a kid being pulled out by a rip current far away, during your final round of the photo competition. Take the winning shot... or run and point the lifeguards to the kid.
ending: You run, the lifeguards reach the kid, and someone else takes a photo of you pointing. That photo wins the competition.
loop: Ends at the stadium, zooming in on a phone screen.
facts: Eagles can see about four to five times sharper than humans
Rip currents can pull swimmers away from shore faster than an Olympic swimmer
visuals: stadium, zoom circle overlay, skyscraper nest, beach, rip current

title: What If You Had a Tail?
opening: What If You Had a Tail? Then: Your tail wags every time your crush walks by. Everyone sees it.
early_wins: Perfect balance, a third hand for snacks, and you can never hide being excited.
mystery_and_reveal: Every human starts with a tail. Before you were born you had one for a few weeks, and your tailbone is what's left of it.
climax: Your friend is about to fall off a climbing wall, and your tail can reach where your arms can't. But it'll hurt.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: Human embryos have a tail for a few weeks; the tailbone is its remnant

title: What If You Felt Every Emotion 10x Stronger?
hook: A dog food advert comes on and you're sobbing on a crowded bus.
rule: Every feeling hits ten times harder, the good ones and the bad ones.
beats: A joke makes you laugh until you can't breathe
A single bad grade feels like the end of the world
Love songs are now dangerous
climax: Your best friend Leo is moving away tomorrow. Saying goodbye will hurt ten times more than for anyone else. Skip the goodbye... or go anyway.
ending: You go, you both cry, and it hurts like nothing ever has. But the hug feels ten times better too.
loop: Ends on the bus, a dog food advert starting.
facts: Emotional tears have a different chemical makeup from tears caused by onions
Strong emotions trigger adrenaline, which speeds up your heart and breathing
visuals: bus, tears, laughter, report card, airport goodbye

title: What If Your Arms Could Think for Themselves?
opening: What If Your Arms Could Think for Themselves? Then: Your left hand finishes your homework while you're still asleep.
early_wins: Each arm has its own opinions: one wants pizza, one wants salad.
mystery_and_reveal: Octopuses actually work like this. About two-thirds of their brain cells are in their arms, so each arm can make its own decisions. Now your arms argue with you.
climax: At the climbing gym, your friend falls, and your arms disagree about whether to catch him.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: About two-thirds of an octopus's neurons are in its arms

title: What If You Could Hold Your Breath for an Hour?
hook: You win the swimming pool breath-holding contest. The second-place kid gave up forty minutes ago.
rule: Your lungs last an hour, but the rest of you still gets cold, scared and tired underwater.
beats: You watch a whole movie underwater
Lifeguards hate you
Your record is longer than any human's, and nobody believes you
climax: Your friend's car keys and phone fall to the bottom of a deep, dark quarry lake, and so does his little sister's beloved teddy bear. You can only search for one before you're too cold. The keys and phone... or the bear.
ending: You come up with the bear. She hugs it soaking wet. Your friend sighs and orders new keys.
loop: Ends at the pool contest starting again.
facts: The record for holding your breath is over 24 minutes, after breathing pure oxygen first
Cold water triggers the 'diving reflex', which slows your heart to save oxygen
visuals: swimming pool, stopwatch, quarry lake, teddy bear

title: What If You Never Got Tired Running?
opening: What If You Never Got Tired Running? Then: You go for a jog after breakfast and come home for dinner.
early_wins: You win every marathon. You run to school, to the next town, to the beach.
mystery_and_reveal: Humans already are the best long-distance runners on Earth, because we sweat so well. Our ancestors could chase animals until they collapsed from heat. But never feeling tired means never knowing when your joints are breaking down.
climax: A wildfire blocks the only road out of town, and someone has to run to the next village for help.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: Humans are exceptional endurance runners, partly because we cool down by sweating

title: What If You Could See Ultraviolet?
hook: You look at a plain yellow flower and see glowing landing strips painted on it for bees.
rule: You see a hidden layer of the world, but UV light is also what damages eyes.
beats: You spot exactly where your friend missed with sunscreen
Fake money looks obviously fake to you
Sunny days are dazzling, so you need special glasses
climax: Your little brother Sam's favourite cat goes missing at night. Searching with a UV torch means staring at UV light that could hurt your eyes. Protect your eyes... or find the cat.
ending: You spot the cat's glowing trail, find her stuck under a shed, and Sam names his next kitten after you.
loop: Ends looking at a yellow flower in the garden.
facts: Many flowers have ultraviolet patterns that guide bees to nectar
Some people whose eye lens has been removed in surgery can see a little ultraviolet light
visuals: flower with glowing UV pattern, sunscreen patches, UV torch, cat

title: What If You Could Jump 10x Higher?
opening: What If You Could Jump 10x Higher? Then: You jump for a basketball and land on the school roof.
early_wins: Shortcuts over buildings, fruit from the top of the tree, the end of every elevator.
mystery_and_reveal: A flea can jump many times its own body length. But what goes up comes down: landing from ten times higher hits your knees with enormous force.
climax: A kitten is stuck on a high ledge. Getting it means a landing your knees might not survive.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: Fleas can jump many times their own body length

title: What If Your Hair Grew 100x Faster?
hook: You get a fresh haircut in the morning. By lunch you have a ponytail.
rule: Hair growth uses protein. Growing this fast, your body is always running low.
beats: Barbers know you by name, and you go three times a day
You sell your hair for wigs and make a fortune
Your eyebrows need trimming before every exam
climax: A kids' cancer charity collects hair for wigs, and you could donate enough for dozens of kids. But it's the day of your big photo shoot as a model. The shoot... or the kids.
ending: You donate, and by evening it's grown back anyway. A little girl sends you a photo in her new wig. Best photo shoot you've ever had.
loop: Ends in the barber's chair, morning, fresh haircut.
facts: Hair normally grows about a centimetre a month
Hair is made of keratin, a protein, so growing it uses up protein from your diet
visuals: barber chair, clock, ponytail, wigs, photo shoot

title: What If Your Skin Showed Your Feelings?
opening: What If Your Skin Showed Your Feelings? Then: Your crush says hi and you turn bright pink. Not your cheeks. All of you.
early_wins: No more lying about being fine. Poker is impossible.
mystery_and_reveal: Octopuses and cuttlefish change color in a split second using cells called chromatophores. Humans have a small version: blushing. Now everyone can read you.
climax: Your best friend asks if you like her new song. Your skin answers before you can.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: Octopuses and cuttlefish change skin color using cells called chromatophores

title: What If Your Balance Was Perfect?
hook: You walk across a rope between two buildings, eating a sandwich, on your first try.
rule: Your inner ear is perfect, but it disagrees with your eyes, so cars and boats make you sick.
beats: You stand on a moving bus without holding anything
You become a skateboard legend in a week
Car rides make you throw up because your eyes and ears disagree
climax: A cat is stuck on a thin, swaying branch over a river. You're the only one who can reach it, but it means missing the bus to your tightrope competition. The competition... or the cat.
ending: You save the cat, and the owner drives you to the competition. You throw up in the car, then win.
loop: Ends on the rope between buildings again.
facts: Your sense of balance comes from fluid-filled tubes in your inner ear
Motion sickness happens when your eyes and inner ear send your brain different signals
visuals: rope between buildings, bus, skateboard, tree over river

title: What If You Could See Germs?
opening: What If You Could See Germs? Then: You look at your phone screen and put it down forever.
early_wins: You see dust mites in your pillow, bacteria on your hands, mold before it shows.
mystery_and_reveal: You carry roughly as many bacterial cells as human cells, tens of trillions, and most of them help you. But try eating anything once you've seen it.
climax: Your grandma's kitchen has a contamination nobody can see, right before the family dinner.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: The human body hosts tens of trillions of bacteria, roughly as many as its own cells

title: What If You Had 360-Degree Vision?
hook: Your teacher writes on the board and says, 'Who's texting?' You answer, without turning around.
rule: Eyes on the sides of your head see everything, but they lose depth. You can't judge distance.
beats: Nobody can ever sneak up on you
You can't catch a ball because you can't tell how far away it is
Pouring water into a glass is a disaster
climax: In a crowded mall, you see a little kid wander toward the escalator behind you while you're on stage collecting a prize. Accept the prize... or jump off stage.
ending: You jump off, scoop the kid up before the escalator, and get the prize later from the mall manager, who doubles it.
loop: Ends back in class, teacher asking 'who's texting?'
facts: Rabbits and horses can see almost all the way around themselves
Judging depth needs two eyes looking at the same thing from slightly different angles
visuals: classroom, vision cone overlay, ball, mall stage, escalator

title: What If You Never Needed to Drink Water?
opening: What If You Never Needed to Drink Water? Then: You cross a desert with a sandwich and no bottle.
early_wins: No thirst, no bathroom breaks, no water bills.
mystery_and_reveal: Your body is about sixty percent water, and you'd normally survive only a few days without drinking. Thirst is the alarm that keeps you alive, and you've lost it.
climax: On a long hike, your friends' water runs out. You have the only full bottles, and they're heavy.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: The human body is roughly 60% water
Most people can survive only a few days without water

title: What If You Could Sense Electricity Like a Shark?
hook: You find your friend hiding in the dark during hide and seek because you can feel his heartbeat's electricity.
rule: You feel every electric field, so cities feel like constant static.
beats: You know which wires are live without a tester
Phones buzzing in pockets feel like bees
Thunderstorms give you a headache days in advance
climax: After a storm, a power line falls near a playground. You can feel exactly where the dangerous ground is, but getting close will feel like screaming in your head. Stay away... or guide the kids out safely.
ending: You walk the kids out along the only safe path and the power company says you saved lives. That night, for the first time, the city feels quiet.
loop: Ends at hide and seek in the dark.
facts: Sharks can detect the tiny electric fields made by the muscles of their prey
Your own heart produces electrical signals, which is what an ECG measures
visuals: dark room, glowing electric field lines, wires, storm, playground

title: What If Half Your Brain Could Sleep at a Time?
opening: What If Half Your Brain Could Sleep at a Time? Then: You sleep with one eye open. Literally.
early_wins: You can rest while gaming, watch a movie while half asleep, and never lose a full night.
mystery_and_reveal: Dolphins really do this. They sleep one half of the brain at a time, so they can keep swimming and breathing. But half-asleep you says the weirdest things.
climax: Your little brother is scared of a storm. Sleeping fully means missing it if he needs you.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: Dolphins sleep with one half of the brain at a time

title: What If Your Metabolism Was 10x Faster?
hook: You eat a whole birthday cake for breakfast and you're hungry again by nine.
rule: Burning energy ten times faster means you're always hot, always hungry, and you crash if you skip a meal.
beats: You never get cold
Food costs more than rent
At night your body slows down so much you can barely wake up
climax: You're on a mountain hike when a storm traps your group overnight with very little food. You need far more than anyone else. Eat your share... or give it to the kid who's shivering.

title: What If You Could Regrow Body Parts?
opening: What If You Could Regrow Body Parts? Then: You lose a tooth, and a new one is there by lunch.
early_wins: Broken bones, lost fingertips, bad knees: all replaceable.
mystery_and_reveal: The axolotl, a Mexican salamander, can regrow whole legs, parts of its heart, even parts of its brain. Scientists study it to learn how. But regrowing takes huge amounts of energy.
climax: Your friend loses a finger in an accident. Scientists say studying you could help him, if you give up a year of your life to tests.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: Axolotls can regrow limbs and parts of organs

title: What If You Could Taste With Your Hands?
hook: You shake hands with a stranger and immediately know he had garlic bread for lunch.
rule: Everything you touch, you taste. There's no off switch.
beats: Holding the bus rail is the worst thing you've ever tasted
You can taste whether fruit is ripe just by touching it
Gloves are your best friend
climax: In a chemistry lab, you touch a bottle labelled water and taste something sharp and bitter: it's not water, and a classmate is about to drink from an identical bottle. Keep quiet and avoid looking weird... or knock it out of their hand.
ending: You knock it away, the teacher tests it, and it's a cleaning chemical someone mislabeled. From then on, everyone lets you check their drinks.
loop: Ends shaking hands with a stranger.
facts: Catfish have taste buds all over their bodies
Octopuses taste with the suckers on their arms

title: What If Your Bones Were Made of Steel?
opening: What If Your Bones Were Made of Steel? Then: You walk into a door frame and the door frame loses.
early_wins: Nothing breaks: falls, crashes, football tackles.
mystery_and_reveal: Steel is about four times denser than bone, so you're suddenly much heavier. Chairs break, floors creak, and you can never, ever swim again.
climax: Your friend falls into a lake and you're the closest one. You'd sink like an anchor.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: Steel is several times denser than bone

title: What If You Could Feel Which Way Is North?
opening: What If You Could Feel Which Way Is North? Then: You've never been lost in your life. Not once.
early_wins: You navigate forests, cities and cave tours with your eyes closed.
mystery_and_reveal: Birds use Earth's magnetic field to migrate thousands of kilometers, and a 2019 study found human brainwaves react to magnetic changes too, even though we don't notice. Now magnets and phones make you dizzy.
climax: Your class gets lost in a forest at night with dead phones, and you're the only compass.
ending: End on the debate question (e.g. 'Would you take it? Yes or no?') so it loops back to the opening title question.
facts: Many migrating birds can sense Earth's magnetic field

title: What If You Couldn't Feel Pain?
hook: You lean on the stove to grab the salt. The whole kitchen smells like burning... and you only notice when your friend screams.
rule: Pain is your body's alarm system. Without it, nothing tells you when you're getting hurt.
beats: Football tackle, you get straight up and keep playing... with a broken wrist you won't discover for a week
You win every dare: ice bath, hot sauce, cactus hug
Your friends start checking YOU for injuries because you can't
climax: A pan of boiling oil tips toward your little brother Sam. You can grab it bare-handed without flinching, but your hands will be badly burned and you won't feel how bad. The trophy-winning pitching arm... or Sam.
ending: You grab it, Sam is safe, and at the hospital the doctor asks how much it hurts. 'I don't know,' you say, which is the scariest answer there is.
loop: Last line lands you back in the kitchen, leaning toward the stove again.
facts: People born unable to feel pain (congenital insensitivity to pain) exist, and they often injure themselves without noticing
Your hand pulls away from a hot surface by a spinal reflex, before your brain even registers the pain
visuals: kitchen, smoke wisps, football field, cast on arm, ice bath, hospital
note: A popular channel already made 'What if you couldn't feel pain?' with a twist where the pain goes to whoever loves you most. Ours must use a completely different twist (the science angle: pain is an alarm), never theirs.
